text: In 2003, there was no new Star Wars movie. And no new Harry Potter movie.
LEGO's sales fell by about a quarter. In the United States, by about a third. More than half of the drop came from the movie sets. And stores that had stocked up the year before now ordered less.
That's when the hidden cost showed up. Every one of those thousands of molds, bins and production runs still had to be paid for, whether a set sold or not.

In January 2004, LEGO announced a record loss for 2003: about one point four billion kroner before tax. The turnaround manager left. Kjeld Kirk Kristiansen took over the day-to-day running of the company himself.

When the finance team went through the company product by product, they found something worse. About sixty percent of sales were producing all of the company's operating profit. Everything else, together, was losing money. One finance executive later said LEGO had been destroying value since 1993.
And 2004 was turning out even worse. For the first time, it was a real question whether LEGO, as an independent family company, would survive.
